briteiros.name: Citânia de Briteiros
briteiros.short: A Celtic Iron Age hill fort on Monte de São Romão, rediscovered by Martins Sarmento in 1874–1875
briteiros.long: The Citânia de Briteiros is a large fortified settlement of the Castro culture on Monte de São Romão, 15 kilometres north of Guimarães. The site covers about 24 hectares, of which roughly seven are open to visitors. It flourished in the 2nd–1st centuries BC, and after the Roman conquest life here faded by the 2nd century AD. The first excavations were begun in 1875 by Francisco Martins Sarmento, who uncovered the acropolis and rebuilt two dwellings. Four lines of wall survive, along with about a hundred family compounds, two public baths with the carved Pedra Formosa slab, and a council house. In 1910 the site was declared a national monument.
briteiros.history:
The Citânia de Briteiros is a fortified settlement, or castro, of the Castro culture, on the summit of Monte de São Romão (336 m) above the Ave river. The hill had been inhabited since the Neolithic and Chalcolithic, and at the beginning of the 1st millennium BC it was a favoured place for Atlantic Bronze Age rock engravings. The castro itself came later: most of the ruins visible today date from the second Iron Age, especially the last two centuries BC. Its inhabitants are believed to have been Celtic.

Around the 1st century AD the settlement was occupied by Roman settlers. The evidence lies in coin finds — most often of Augustus and Tiberius, more rarely Republican, Flavian and Antonine — as well as amphorae and red pottery. Romanisation shows in the layout of the alleys and buildings on the eastern slope, but the Roman impact overall is weak. From the 1st century AD the number of finds falls away: by the 2nd century very few people were left inside the walls. In the High Middle Ages the hill was briefly reoccupied, with a medieval chapel and graveyard built on the acropolis.

Though the ruins had been known since at least the 16th century, scientific excavation began only in the 1870s. In 1875 the Portuguese archaeologist Francisco Martins Sarmento began annual campaigns while helping to develop methods of archaeological research and preservation in Portugal. He uncovered much of the acropolis, the highest part of the settlement, and rebuilt two dwellings from his findings. His discoveries led him to buy the land on which the settlement stood; he bequeathed it, and his research materials, to the Martins Sarmento Society. From the 1930s to the 1960s new excavations were led by Mário Cardozo, revealing much of the eastern slope and further parts of the acropolis. Further surveys followed in the 1970s and in 2002, 2005 and 2006. In 2004 a project began under the University of Minho with the Martins Sarmento Society to bring the earlier studies together and improve the site's conservation.

In 1910 the Citânia was classified and protected as a Portuguese national monument. It is one of the most important proto-historic settlements on the Iberian Peninsula, thanks to its size, the monumentality of its walls, the architecture of its buildings and its urban organisation. Together with the Citânia de Sanfins, in Paços de Ferreira, it is one of the best sites for studying the Castro culture in the north-west of the country.

The visible ruins form a plan of great size, with four lines of wall and a roughly oval shape. The main platform of the acropolis covers 250 by 150 metres. The walls, one to three metres thick and less than two metres high, are built of dry stone; one stretch restored by Martins Sarmento reaches almost four metres. Gates are cut through each line of wall, some of them still showing the hollows where palisades stood. The streets, unusually for a castro, form a roughly grid-like pattern. About a hundred family compounds have been found inside the walls: each is bounded by a stone wall and contains one to three round stone houses, outbuildings and a paved courtyard where daily work was done. Besides the houses there were water channels from a spring, fountains, two public bath buildings and a large meeting or council house. The carved Pedra Formosa slab, almost three square metres in area, is the best-known find from the northern bath. The population of the acropolis is estimated at about 625, and that of the whole settlement at up to 1,500.

briteiros.tip: The site is open to visitors (usually 9:00–17:30, with seasonal hours) for a small ticket. It can be reached only by car or taxi: about 15 kilometres north of Guimarães on the EN101 and EN310, through São Salvador de Briteiros. Bring water and footwear for the weather — the paths are stony and exposed to the sun. On the way, look in on the Martins Sarmento Society museum in Guimarães, which holds the finds from the site.
